title: Fairmount Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Fairmount wells have a 39 ft median depth; finished well costs are typically $8,000-$14,700, based on local drilling conditions.
h1: Fairmount, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land in Fairmount means looking beyond the house and checking the well record. Within 5 miles of Fairmount, Colorado DWR records include 6,250 permitted wells, though only 3,596 are recorded as constructed. The local numbers show many shallow wells, generally useful production, and a smaller group of deep wells that can change a drilling budget quickly.

Fairmount sits in a mountain setting over ground described in the cost model as Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. Nearby records from Arvada, Applewood, Wheat Ridge, Golden, West Pleasant View, and East Pleasant View help provide context, but a neighboring well is not a guarantee for a particular lot.

sections.heading: Fairmount well depth: shallow records, deep exceptions
sections.html:
The recorded median well depth near Fairmount is 39 feet. The middle half runs from 24 to 125 feet, so a driller's bid based only on the median can be misleading. Seventy percent of recorded wells are under 100 feet, while 14% fall from 100 to 300 feet, 12% from 300 to 600 feet, and 5% are 600 feet or deeper.

The 90th-percentile depth is 400 feet, and the deepest well on record is 1,985 feet. That spread points to substantial variation across short distances. Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with 5,015 wells in that category. Fractured bedrock can be unpredictable, so look at nearby completed wells and their construction reports before accepting a drilling estimate.

sections.heading: How much water Fairmount wells make
sections.html:
Among the 433 wells that report a pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute. The middle half runs from 6.0 to 14.0 gallons per minute. Sixty-six percent report yields from 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 21% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

Low-producing wells are present but not dominant: 10% are in the 1-to-5-gallon-per-minute range and 3% are under 1 gallon per minute. For a buyer, the important limitation is the small reporting pool compared with the total permit record. Ask for the well permit, construction report, pump information, and any production testing rather than relying on a regional median.

sections.heading: Fairmount water levels and the recorded trend
sections.html:
The current combined static-water-level record has a median depth to water of 16 feet, with the middle half from 9 to 62 feet below the surface. That is a measurement taken when a well was static, not a guaranteed pumping level. A pump, storage tank, pressure system, and household demand can all affect how the water system performs.

The decade series does not show a simple steady decline. The median was 24 feet below surface in the 1960s, rose to 118 feet in the 1970s, then measured 13 feet in the 2010s and 12 feet in the 2020s. Only 111 wells report a static water level, so treat the series as local record context, not a site-specific forecast.

sections.heading: Fairmount drilling history and the active names
sections.html:
Permitting has continued through 2025. The record shows 244 permits from the 1950s, 325 from the 1960s, 556 from the 1970s, 415 from the 1980s, 1,047 from the 1990s, 807 from the 2000s, 697 from the 2010s, and 289 from the 2020s. Domestic or household use accounts for 49% of the use mix, while monitoring wells account for 32%.

The most active driller names in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 1,216 records; Adams Water Well Drilling (Adams, George E), with 162; and John'S Drilling Inc. (John, Lloyd), with 156. Those counts describe permit records, not a current recommendation or proof that a driller is available for a new project.

sections.heading: What a new Fairmount well may cost
sections.html:
The local drilling model uses a typical rate of $50 to $70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 39-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $2,000 to $2,700. That is only the hole, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $8,000 to $14,700. The depth range matters: a parcel near the 400-foot 90th percentile will not price like a median-depth job. Get a written bid that identifies drilling depth assumptions, casing and grout, pump equipment, trench length, electrical work, testing, and what happens if the hole is dry or produces less than expected.

sections.heading: Fairmount risks to check before closing
sections.html:
Water quality deserves its own investigation. Within about 10 miles, the mapped environmental record includes 308 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 164 historic mine features, and 46 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped sites do not establish contamination at a specific property, but they are a reason to test the existing well and understand the property's location relative to them.

Low yield, a dry hole, poor construction, and septic setbacks can also affect a building plan. Confirm the DWR permit and use limits, inspect casing and grout information, and have the existing pump system evaluated. If the property needs a new septic system, verify that the proposed house, well, septic area, driveway, and other improvements can fit together before buying.

sections.heading: A practical Fairmount plan for buyers and builders
sections.html:
Start with the nearest permitted wells, not just the regional statistics. Compare their depths, reported yields, static levels, aquifer descriptions, and construction records. Records from Golden, Wheat Ridge, Arvada, Applewood, West Pleasant View, and East Pleasant View can add context, but the closest comparable wells deserve the most attention.

For an existing home, make the purchase contingent on reviewing the permit, testing the water, checking flow and pressure, and confirming the well's permitted use. For raw land, price the likely complete system rather than only drilling. Colorado DWR permitting, household-use exemptions, pumping limits, augmentation requirements in over-appropriated basins, and septic approval can all affect what the lot can support. Have the driller and septic designer review the site together.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Fairmount, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth near Fairmount is 39 feet, and the middle half runs from 24 to 125 feet. Seventy percent are under 100 feet, but the 90th-percentile depth is 400 feet and the deepest record is 1,985 feet. Nearby wells are useful for estimating a lot, but the range is wide enough to require site-specific review.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Fairmount?
faq.a: The local model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 39-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $2,000 to $2,700. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $8,000 to $14,700. A deeper-than-typical hole, difficult access, or a dry result can change the actual bid.

faq.q: How much water do Fairmount wells produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a median of 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 6.0 to 14.0 gallons per minute. Sixty-six percent are reported between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. However, only 433 wells report a pump yield, so a buyer should review the specific well's test and equipment rather than use the median as a guarantee.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Fairmount, Colorado?
faq.a: The regional map includes 308 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 164 historic mine features, and 46 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those figures do not prove a particular well is unsafe. Test the property's water, review nearby environmental information, and check the well's construction and maintenance history before relying on it for household use.

faq.q: Are Fairmount water levels going down?
faq.a: The reported decade medians do not show a steady decline. Static water depth was 24 feet below surface in the 1960s, 118 feet in the 1970s, 13 feet in the 2010s, and 12 feet in the 2020s. Only 111 wells report static water levels, so this is regional record context rather than proof of current conditions at a particular Fairmount property.
